name: Watubela
world_status: statement found in an open source

earlier_scan.source_named: Glottolog lists only 19th-century wordlists (Turner 1884; von Rosenberg 1867/1878); no grammar or phonology of Watubela located.

new_statements.quote: With regard to the phonetic notation, stress is penultimate unless otherwise marked.
new_statements.citation: Collins, James T. 1986. Eastern Seram: a subgrouping argument. In Paul Geraghty, Lois Carrington & S.A. Wurm (eds), FOCAL II: Papers from the Fourth International Conference on Austronesian Linguistics, 123-146. Pacific Linguistics C-94. Canberra: Australian National University. DOI 10.15144/PL-C94.123
new_statements.locator: p. 141 (Appendix: A comparative wordlist of the languages of Eastern Seram, second paragraph); PDF page 13 of the chapter file, page 147 of; Watubela stress-marked forms on pp. 142-145
new_statements.rule_in_words: Default word stress on the penultimate syllable; a small number of words (marked with an acute in the wordlist) have final stress.
new_statements.exceptions: Non-penultimate stress is 'otherwise marked' in the lists: in the Watubela column a few words carry an acute on the final syllable (read from the page image: mamán 'say', katlú 'egg', malá: 'long', kotnáu 'where', laŋit ni tái 'cloud', sabóu 'sit'), so final stress occurs in a minority of lexical items.
new_statements.domain_note: Word level, citation forms in a 200-item comparative wordlist; the statement is a transcription convention covering all six languages of the appendix (Seti, Bobot, Masiwang, Geser, Watubela, Banda), with the Watubela data from Efa village (Watubela Island) and occasional Keldor (K) forms; it is Collins's own field data (two years of fieldwork), not a phonological analysis.
new_statements.identity_note: Collins 1986's Watubela data are from Efa village on Watubela Island proper (with some forms from Keldor, marked K); Ethnologue/Glottolog treat Kesui (Kasiui) and Watubela as dialects of the single language watu1247, so no separate glottocode applies. The 19th-century 'Matabello' wordlists (Wallace 1869) are, per Collins 1986 fn.7, from Kesui island, and von Rosenberg 1867 p.106 already reports a dialect difference between Kassoewie (Kesui) and Watoebella. The stress statement is a notation convention that Collins applies jointly to all six Eastern Seram languages in his appendix, not a Watubela-specific phonological analysis.

sources.locator: p. 141 (Appendix: A comparative wordlist of the languages of Eastern Seram, second paragraph); PDF page 13 of the chapter file, page 147 of; Watubela stress-marked forms on pp. 142-145
sources.note: Comparative/subgrouping paper with a 200-item wordlist of six Eastern Seram languages incl. Watubela (Efa village; K = Keldor). Appendix p.141: 'With regard to the phonetic notation, stress is penultimate unless otherwise marked.' In the Watubela column (pp.142-145) a handful of words carry an acute on the final syllable (as read from the page image: mamán 'say', katlú 'egg', malá: 'long', kotnáu 'where', laŋit ni tái 'cloud', sabóu 'sit'), i.e. marked exceptions with final stress. Body of the paper discusses only segmental sound changes (e.g. *a > o in the penultimate syllable).

sources.citation: Turner, George. 1884. Samoa, a hundred years ago and long before. London: Macmillan. (comparative vocabulary with a 'Matabello' column)
sources.note: Comparative vocabulary only (Matabello forms such as Olér Wulan, Aridin, Dar Phidi); no accent remarks anywhere in the scanned text.

sources.citation: von Rosenberg, C.B.H. 1878. Der Malayische Archipel: Land und Leute in Schilderungen. Leipzig: Gustav Weigel. (Die Watubella-Inseln pp.355ff; II. Vergleichendes Wörterverzeichniss pp.597ff with a Watubella column)
sources.note: Travel account plus a comparative wordlist (21 columns incl. Watubella). Grep of the scanned for Betonung/Accent/Sprache in the Watubella chapter and wordlist found no remark on stress (the wordlist tables are scanned-garbled).

sources.citation: Glottolog 5.1 languoid page watu1247 (Watubela); Wikipedia 'Watubela language'
sources.note: Glottolog cites only Collins 1986 for subclassification (plus Ethnologue 2025 for status); names Esiriun, Kasiui, Kasui, Kesui, Matabello, Snabi Watubela, Wesi. Wikipedia cites Collins 1986, Loski & Loski 1989 and Grimes & Edwards (2026, survey of the Austronesian languages of eastern Indonesia and Timor-Leste); neither says anything about stress. Crossref/Garuda queries for 'Watubela' returned only non-linguistic Indonesian local-government papers; searches done via Crossref, OpenAlex (429), Google Books API (quota 0), archive.org and Wayback).

sources.citation: Cowan, H.K.J. 1957. Een Russisch gegeven over de taal van Watubella. Bijdragen tot de Taal-, Land- en Volkenkunde 113(3): 290-291. DOI 10.1163/22134379-90002289 (open access, CC BY-NC 3.0)
sources.note: Two-page note reproducing Miklucho-Maclay's 49-word Watubella list of 25 Feb 1874 (from the 1950 Russian edition of his works, vol. 2 pp. 34-35), re-transcribed from Cyrillic, with a remark that the language is Austronesian (or heavily Austronesian-influenced). Nothing on stress or accent; no accent marks in the list.

sources.citation: Wallace, Alfred R. 1869. The Malay Archipelago, vol. 2. London: Macmillan. Appendix: vocabularies (no. 45 'Matabello'; per Collins 1986 fn.7 collected on Kesui island)
sources.note: Wordlist only. General note to the vocabularies: 'Long, short, and accented syllables are marked in the usual way'; the Matabello column shows a few accented forms in the scanned (e.g. 'Léburr', 'Aow lémi', 'Halétalte', 'Niféa') but there is no statement about Watubela stress.

sources.citation: von Rosenberg, C.B.H. 1867. Reis naar de Zuidoostereilanden, gedaan in 1865 op last der regering van Nederlandsch-Indië. 's-Gravenhage: Nijhoff. (ch. X De Watoebella-Eilanden pp.90ff; Vergelijkende woordenlijst van de tongvallen der Zuidoostereilanden pp.105ff)
sources.note: Short comparative wordlist with a Watoebella column. p.106: the Tijoor and Watoebella lists are too short to draw conclusions; a dialect difference between Kassoewie (Kesui) and Watoebella is reported. p.107: French accents on e and breve/macron signs mark vowel quality and length, not stress. No stress statement.
